newsitem.title: JAPAN: No problem to start EMU with fewer members--Gaddum.
newsitem.headline: No problem to start EMU with fewer members--Gaddum.

text.p: It would be no problem to launch European economic and monetary union (EMU) with a smaller number of countries if that provided stability, Bundesbank Vice-President Johann-Wilhelm Gaddum said on Tuesday.
"There's nothing wrong with starting with a smaller range of participants if that makes it easier to launch a real community of stability," he told a Tokyo symposium on EMU.
He also said it is possible that not all European countries will join the EMU from its inception at the beginning of 1999.
"The choice of countries that has to be made in the spring of 1998 may mean that only a few countries join the European monetary union in the first round."
But he said the Maastricht treaty on EMU gives other nations the right to join at a later stage.

Gaddum also said it would be difficult for Germany to meet its self-imposed target of limiting its deficit for the current year to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) because of the situation in its job market.

"The German government has set itself the target of limiting the deficit of the current year to 2.9 percent of the GDP and continuing to reduce it even further subsequently," he said, adding that the size of the task had grown bigger because of the unfavourable labour market situation.
"For that reason it will be certainly not easy to achieve this self-imposed target," Gaddum said.
Economic targets to qualify for the EMU single currency club set under the 1992 Maastricht treaty include a budget deficit lower than three percent of GDP.
